sections.html:
Farmington is the Davis County seat, set between Ogden and Salt Lake City with a commute of about a half hour to job centers in both. The 2020 census counted 24,531 people, up from 18,275 in 2010, and most homes are owned by the people living in them. That mix of steady demand and rising values is why many owners here have real equity, and why a few of them still run into old tax bills, unpermitted basement apartments or a valuation they dislike before they list.

This page covers the local items that tend to decide how a sale goes: the county tax calendar, the appeal process, the city's accessory unit rules and what a direct cash sale looks like from start to finish.

sections.h2: Property tax due dates and penalties
sections.html:
Farmington parcels are billed through Davis County, on dates set by the Utah calendar. The bill is due November 30. After that day an unpaid balance is delinquent, but the penalty shrinks if you clear the whole amount by January 31.

Primary homes get a 45% residential exemption, so a house you live in is taxed on 55% of its market value. A rental or second home does not get that break, which is worth remembering if you are selling a property you moved out of.

The county's Tax Administration office is at 61 South Main Street, Room 101, in the county seat. The phone number is 801-451-3331.

The Davis County Controller mails the Notice of Assessors' Property Market Valuation at the end of July. If the value looks too high, you can appeal to the Board of Equalization, which is the Davis County Commission. The filing deadline falls in mid-September, so call Tax Administration at 801-451-3331 for the exact date before you file.

Only the market value can be appealed, not the tax rate. The owner or an agent with a notarized authorization must file. Strong evidence includes:

  • closing documents signed by the title agent,
  • a full appraisal by a certified appraiser,
  • sales of at least three comparable properties near January 1,
  • documented factual errors, such as the wrong square footage.

If you plan to sell soon, a lower assessed value only helps while you own the house, so weigh the effort against how long you will hold it.

Farmington allows two kinds of accessory units and a third route that lets an owner put a detached unit on its own lot. Only one ADU is allowed per single-family home.

  • Internal ADU: inside or attached to the main home, on a lot of at least 6,000 square feet.
  • Detached ADU: a permanent structure on a foundation, on a lot of at least 10,000 square feet.
  • Subordinate single-family dwelling: a separate lot with its own home, subject to subdivision approval.

Either the main home or the ADU must be owner-occupied. A subordinate dwelling must be owner-occupied for two years after ownership is separated from the main home. Each unit needs its own full kitchen and bathroom plus one off-street parking space beyond the main home's, and rentals must run 30 days or longer, so an ADU cannot be a short-term rental.

Converting space for an internal ADU takes a building permit unless the space was already approved for residential occupancy. A basement unit with no paperwork can stall a sale that depends on a mortgage, because a lender's appraiser will ask about it.

Farmington has real winters, and lake-enhanced snow can arrive in the cold months. Flash floods have hit the town in past decades, so a lot near a creek or canyon mouth deserves a second look. The Farmington Area Pressurized Irrigation District has served homeowners since July 1978, and buyers often ask whether a lot is on that system.

  • Ask your insurance agent whether a flood policy applies to a parcel near a creek or canyon mouth.
  • Keep the roof age and any snow or water damage repairs on paper.
  • Note whether the yard uses pressurized irrigation.

sections.h2: How does a cash sale work in Farmington?
sections.html:
Without a lender in the picture, a cash sale skips the appraisal, the loan underwriting and the financing contingency that can unravel a deal late. You describe the house, we study it alongside recent nearby sales, and the offer is yours to take or leave.

  1. Send us the address and a few details about the house.
  2. We look over the property and the surrounding blocks.
  3. You say yes or no to the offer, with no obligation.
  4. A title company searches the record and picks a closing date with you.
  5. The deed is recorded and the funds reach you at closing.

You choose the closing date within what the title company needs, so a move can be timed around a new job, a school year or a purchase elsewhere. There are no showings, no staging and no repair list to negotiate.

sections.h2: Selling with taxes owed or an unpermitted unit
sections.html:
If the tax bill is unpaid or an ADU never got its permit, tell the title company early. Back taxes are normally paid out of the sale proceeds at closing, and the title search will show them either way, so surprises help nobody.

Farmington owners who talk to us usually describe one of these:

  • An older house in or near the historic district that needs updating.
  • A basement apartment that was never permitted as an internal ADU.
  • A detached unit the owner wants to sell separately, which the city treats as a subordinate single-family dwelling needing subdivision approval.
  • A valuation notice the owner disagrees with and wants to appeal before selling.

Each of these can slow a traditional listing. A direct sale lets you skip staging and repair work and move on the timeline you choose.

sections.h2: What to gather before you call
sections.html: A folder of paperwork shortens the road to closing. Pull your most recent tax notice, the valuation notice if it arrived in July, any permits for additions or a basement unit, and records of roof or water repairs. If you rent a unit, have the lease terms handy, since the 30-day minimum applies to ADU rentals here. A recent mortgage statement helps the title company work out the payoff, and a photo of the roof, the furnace and any basement kitchen lets us give you a realistic offer on the first call. If someone else lives in the house, tell us at the start so timing and access are clear to everyone.

faqs.q: What county is Farmington, Utah in?
faqs.a: Davis County. Farmington is the county seat, and the county's Tax Administration office is at 61 South Main Street, Room 101.

faqs.q: When are property taxes due in Farmington?
faqs.a: November 30, the statewide due date. Taxes unpaid after that date become delinquent, with a reduced penalty if everything is paid by January 31.

faqs.q: How do I appeal my Farmington property value?
faqs.a: File with the Davis County Board of Equalization after the valuation notice arrives at the end of July. The deadline is in mid-September, so call Tax Administration for the exact date. You can appeal only the market value.

faqs.q: Can I rent out a Farmington ADU for short stays?
faqs.a: No. Farmington requires ADU rentals to be 30 days or longer, and the owner must live in either the main home or the ADU.

faqs.q: What size lot do I need for a detached ADU in Farmington?
faqs.a: At least 10,000 square feet. An internal ADU needs a lot of at least 6,000 square feet.
